name: Chin reduction / shaving

card.summary: Surgery to shrink a large chin by burring the bone or moving it back and up; documented in surgical papers, with nerve and contour risks.
card.aka: Reduction genioplasty, chin shaving, submental ostectomy
card.note: Surgeons list mental nerve injury, bony irregularity and chin pad ptosis as potential sequelae.

quick.overview:
Chin reduction is surgery to make a long, protruding or wide chin smaller. The two classical approaches are an osteotomy that moves the chin bone back or up, and burring (shaving) the surface of the bone.

The published evidence is made up of technique descriptions and case series, including work on setback with reduction genioplasty for long chins and on feminization surgery.
quick.mechanism: A segment of chin bone can be cut and repositioned (reduction or setback genioplasty), or prominent bone can be burred down. Another described approach removes bone and soft tissue from under the chin.
quick.risks: Surgical papers state that both main approaches have potential negative aesthetic sequelae, including mental nerve injury, bony contour irregularities, increased submental soft-tissue fullness and chin pad ptosis. It is performed under anaesthetic by licensed surgeons.

chain: Chin bone is moved back, shortened, narrowed or burred down
Chin projection, height or width decreases
Profile and lower third sit in better proportion with the nose, lips and jaw
angle.text: People with a long, protruding or wide chin use reduction surgery to change the shape of the lower face directly. Surgeons describe the aim as bringing the chin into balance with the rest of the profile, and in some cases combining it with jaw surgery or feminization procedures.

lead: Chin reduction refers to surgical procedures that reduce the size of the chin in projection, height or width. A 1999 paper states that, at that time, surgical reduction of an isolated large chin was not a simple procedure, and that two operations existed: osteotomy with setback, or reduction of the prominence by burring. [1] In looksmaxxing vocabulary the topic sits under 'hardmaxxing', the group of bone-altering procedures, and is usually discussed alongside jaw surgery, chin implants and facial feminization.

The chin is the lowest part of the mandible, and its position strongly shapes the side profile. Surgeons treat it as one component of lower-face balance, assessed together with the nose, lips, jaw and bite. [10][11] Reduction genioplasty is used for an isolated large chin and is also combined with mandibular setback for prognathism (a jaw that sits forward) with a long chin. [2][3] A box-shaped chin impaction osteotomy has been reported as part of mandibular feminization surgery. [4]

The literature on chin reduction consists of technique papers, case series and surgeon-reported outcomes; no randomized trials comparing chin-reduction techniques were found. [1][5] Chin reduction is far less commonly discussed than chin augmentation, which has a larger body of work on implants and sliding advancement. [12][13]

paras: The chin (genium) is the bony prominence at the front of the mandible, covered by the chin pad and the mentalis muscle, which lifts the lower lip and chin. [12] Reduction procedures can shorten the chin vertically, pull it backward, or narrow it from side to side. Which approach is used depends on whether the issue is projection, height, width or an overall long lower face. [5]

Wikipedia's article on chin augmentation describes the mirror image of augmentation: in a sliding osteotomy, a piece of the lower mandible is moved backward rather than forward to reduce projection, and a Korean-developed T-osteotomy removes a trapezoid-shaped section to lengthen and narrow the chin by a few millimetres. [12][11]

In a sliding or reduction genioplasty, the surgeon cuts a segment of the lower chin bone through an incision inside the mouth, repositions it back or up, and fixes it with plates and screws. [11] A 1985 paper described a 'physiological' approach to genioplasty, and a 1975 paper described chin reduction as part of profileplasty. [6][7]

Reports on mandibular setback combined with reduction genioplasty describe improved chin profile in patients with prognathism and a long chin, and a 2020 paper reviews reduction genioplasty in this skeletal setting. [2][3] Reviews of genioplasty in orthognathic surgery discuss the techniques, stability, fixation and complications of chin repositioning generally. [10]

Burring means grinding down the surface of the prominent bone with a surgical burr. The 1999 paper lists it as one of the two classical operations for a large chin, alongside osteotomy with setback. [1] Wikipedia's facial feminization article similarly notes that chin height can be shortened by shaving bone or by a sliding genioplasty that removes part of the bone. [14]

The 1999 Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery paper, part of a multi-paper series on chin surgery, presents a new approach of submental ostectomy with soft-tissue excision, aimed at avoiding the sequelae it attributes to the older operations. [1] A later paper in the same series, published in 2007, discusses key parameters for successful reduction of a large chin. [5]

Authors of a 2019 paper state that strong mandibular angles and a heavy chin are perceived as masculine and describe an osteotomy including a box-shaped impaction of the chin symphysis to reduce chin width and height, combined with narrowing of the mandibular base. [4] Facial feminization surgery as a field is traced by Wikipedia to 1982, when surgeon Douglas Ousterhout began developing most of its procedures, and it lists chin shortening and jaw reduction among the standard components. [14]

Potential negative aesthetic sequelae listed for both classical approaches include mental nerve injuries, bony contour irregularities, increased submental soft-tissue fullness and chin pad ptosis (sagging of the chin pad). [1]

Wikipedia's general genioplasty and chin articles list swelling, bruising and temporary lower-lip numbness or weakness as common effects, and infection, bone changes and nerve damage as less common ones, with surgeon experience described as lowering the risk. [11][12] Its facial feminization article names the mental nerve, tooth roots, non-union of bone and the mentalis muscle among the structures at risk. [14] In orthognathic surgery more broadly, numbness from inferior alveolar nerve injury is a known complication that is usually temporary and rarely permanent. [15]

Recovery after chin osteotomy is described as involving a period of soft foods and limited chewing, with the mentalis muscle reattached carefully. [11] Full bone union after jaw osteotomies is reported to take several months. [15]

Separately from bone reduction, submental fullness from fat has been the subject of registered trials of deoxycholic acid injection, injectable and device treatments, which address soft tissue under the chin rather than the chin bone. [8][9] These are sometimes grouped with chin reduction in online discussion because a fuller neck can make a chin look larger or less defined.

Published work includes technique descriptions and case reports of reduction genioplasty, setback with reduction genioplasty and feminization osteotomy. [1][2][3][4] The 2012 report on setback with reduction genioplasty, the 2020 paper on reduction genioplasty and the 2019 feminization series each describe surgical outcomes in patient groups rather than comparisons with a control. [2][3][4]

Registered trials of submental fat reduction (for example NCT06256445, a phase 3 trial with 252 participants) address soft tissue rather than bone. [9] A sliding osteotomy genioplasty series reporting ten years of experience concerns advancement rather than reduction. [13]

timeline.event: Simon P. Hullihen publishes one of the first reported jaw-surgery cases, the earliest roots of the field that later included genioplasty (per Wikipedia). [15]
Chin reduction in profileplasty described in the Archives of Otolaryngology. [6]
Facial feminization surgery, which includes chin and jaw reduction, begins to be developed by Douglas Ousterhout (per Wikipedia). [14]
Genioplasty: a physiological approach published in Annals of Plastic Surgery. [7]
Submental ostectomy and soft-tissue excision proposed for chin reduction. [1]
Key parameters for successful reduction of a large chin published. [5]
Report on mandibular setback with reduction genioplasty for prognathism and long chin. [2]
Mandibular feminization osteotomy preliminary results published. [4]
Paper on reduction genioplasty for mandibular prognathism and long chin. [3]
